p.src: On the auspicious sixth day of the month, Song Jiang and Lu Junyi prepared to march. Suddenly a report came: the soldiers and people of Yangcheng and Qinshui, two counties under Gaizhou, had repeatedly suffered Tian Hu's ravages and submitted to him only from necessity. Now, learning that the imperial army had arrived, they had seized and bound Kou Fu, the commander defending Yangcheng, and Chen Kai, the commander defending Qinshui, and were escorting them to the army. The elders of both counties led the people forth, bringing sheep and carrying wine, and offered up their cities. Vanguard Commander Song was overjoyed. He richly rewarded the soldiers and people of both places, issued proclamations to reassure them, and restored them to the status of law-abiding subjects. Because Kou Fu and Chen Kai had known the imperial army had arrived yet failed to submit promptly, Vanguard Commander Song ordered them beheaded at once as sacrifices to the banner, to serve as a warning to the rebels. That day both great armies marched out through the northern gate, while Hua Rong and the others laid out wine to bid them farewell. Holding his cup, Song Jiang said to Hua Rong, “Worthy brother, your might strikes fear into the rebel army, and you are well able to serve as this city's bulwark. The city now faces attack only from the north. Should rebel troops appear, use stratagems to strike them and break their courage; then they will not dare cast covetous eyes southward.” Hua Rong and the others assented respectfully and accepted the order. Song Jiang then raised his cup to Lu Junyi and said, “As we march today, we have been blessed with the joyful news that Yangcheng and Qinshui have presented their captives. Now that both places are pacified, worthy brother, you may drive straight on to Jinning, swiftly win great merit, capture the rebel chief Tian Hu alive, repay the imperial court, and share together in wealth and honor.” Lu Junyi replied, “It was through elder brother's awe-inspiring authority that both places submitted without battle. Having received your strict command, how could I dare not exert all my heart and strength!” Song Jiang also took the separate scroll he had earlier ordered Xiao Rang to copy from Xu Guanzhong's map and gave it to Lu Junyi to keep for use when needed. Vanguard Commander Song Jiang then issued orders dividing his troops into three columns: Lin Chong, Suo Chao, Xu Ning, and Zhang Qing were to command ten thousand troops as the vanguard; Sun Li, Zhu Tong, Yan Shun, Ma Lin, Shan Tinggui, Wei Dingguo, Tang Long, and Li Yun were to command ten thousand troops as the rearguard; Song Jiang and Wu Yong were to command the remaining officers and thirty thousand troops as the central army. The three columns, totaling fifty thousand soldiers, advanced toward the northeast. Deputy Vanguard Commander Lu Junyi took leave of Song Jiang, Hua Rong, and the others, then led forty officers and fifty thousand troops northwest on campaign.

p.src: Shan Shiqi shouted, “You bandits from the marsh dare invade our frontier!” From the other side, “Panther Head” Lin Chong spurred out from the ranks and cried, “You wretch who abets tyranny! The armies of Heaven have arrived, yet you still dare resist!” Leveling his spear, he urged his horse straight at Shiqi. The two commanders charged to the center of the field as both armies raised their battle cries. The two mounts crossed, four arms swept to and fro, and eight hooves churned in confusion. After more than fifty bouts neither had gained the advantage, and Lin Chong secretly applauded his opponent’s skill. Seeing that Shiqi could not prevail, Zhu Jing galloped forward, brandishing his saber, to assist him; from the other side, “Featherless Arrow” Zhang Qing raced out to intercept him. The four horsemen fought in two pairs before the battle lines. After Zhang Qing and Zhu Jing had fought for more than twenty bouts, Zhang Qing appeared to weaken, wheeled his horse, and fled. Zhu Jing spurred after him. Zhang Qing steadied his ornate spear, took a stone from his brocade pouch, twisted around, aimed at Zhu Jing’s face, and sent the stone flying with a shout: “Take that!” It struck Zhu Jing squarely on the bridge of the nose. He toppled from his horse, blood spurting forth. Zhang Qing turned his horse and came thrusting with his spear, but Shi Ding and Zhong Liang charged together from the northern ranks and desperately rescued Zhu Jing. When those at the pass saw one of their commanders struck down, they feared that Shiqi might also come to harm and sounded the gong to withdraw. Song Jiang likewise ordered the gong sounded and withdrew his troops to camp. He conferred with Wu Yong, saying, “Today we struck down one of the enemy commanders and somewhat blunted their ardor. But I see that the mountains are steep and the pass is strongly fortified. What sound strategy can we use to break through it?” Lin Chong said, “Tomorrow we shall challenge them at the pass. We must slay that enemy commander, and then all our brothers can mass their strength and storm their way up.” Wu Yong said, “General, you must not act rashly! Master Sun Wu said, ‘Invincibility lies in defense; the possibility of victory lies in attack.’ This means that when the enemy cannot yet be defeated, we should hold our defenses; only when the enemy can be defeated should we attack.” Song Jiang said, “The military adviser speaks most wisely.”

p.src: The next day, Lin Chong and Zhang Qing reported to Vanguard Song and asked to lead troops out to issue a challenge. Song Jiang instructed them, “Even if you win the battle, you must not lightly attempt to storm the pass.” He further ordered Xu Ning and Suo Chao to lead troops in support. Lin Chong and Zhang Qing then led five thousand troops beneath the pass, where they waved their banners, beat their drums, hurled insults, and challenged the enemy. From the Hour of the Dragon until noon, there was no movement atop the pass. Just as Lin Chong and Zhang Qing were about to return to camp, they suddenly heard a cannon blast from within the pass. The gates opened, and Shan Shiqi, together with Wu Su, Shi Ding, Wu Cheng, and Zhong Liang, led twenty thousand troops charging down upon them. Lin Chong said to Zhang Qing, “The enemy means to take advantage of our weariness. Let us summon our strength and press forward.” In the rear, Suo Chao and Xu Ning brought their troops forward together. Both sides formed their ranks and, without exchanging another word, sought out opponents and fell to fighting. Lin Chong fought Wu Su. Shiqi rode forth, and Zhang Qing met him with his pear-blossom spear. Wu Cheng and Shi Ding charged out together, while Suo Chao brandished his ax, leaped his horse forward, and fought both commanders at once. The two armies now raised unceasing battle cries, while seven horsemen, amid clouds of war dust and a gathering aura of slaughter, wheeled and fought in pairs like lanterns spinning in a dance. At the height of the furious battle, “Panther Head” Lin Chong gave a mighty shout and, with a single thrust of his spear, knocked Wu Su from his horse. Though Wu Cheng and Shi Ding were fighting Suo Chao together, they were still overmatched. Seeing Wu Su fall from his horse, Shi Ding hurriedly feigned an opening, whipped his horse around, and fled toward his own lines. When Wu Cheng saw Shi Ding flee the field, he parried the ax and tried to escape, but Suo Chao swung his weapon and cleaved him in two. Seeing that he had lost two commanders, Shan Shiqi wheeled his horse and returned to his ranks. Zhang Qing pursued him and loosed a stone. It struck the back of Shiqi’s helmet with a ringing clang, frightening him so badly that he flattened himself against the saddle and fled. Zhong Liang hurriedly led the troops back toward the pass, but Lin Chong and the others drove their forces in pursuit and routed the northern army. Shan Shiqi led his troops scrambling pell-mell into the pass, scarcely managing to shut the gates in time. Lin Chong and the others fought all the way to the foot of the pass, but arrows and stones rained down from above, preventing them from entering. Lin Chong had already taken an arrow in his left arm, so they withdrew their troops and returned to camp. Song Jiang ordered An Daoquan to treat Lin Chong’s arrow wound. Fortunately, his armor had been thick and the injury was not serious; there is no need to dwell upon it.

p.src: Tang Bin, chief of the Mount Baodu stronghold, was originally a military officer from Pudong. He is brave and upright by nature and long ago swore brotherhood with me, Guan. A powerful magnate framed him. In his fury, Tang Bin killed his enemy, and the authorities pursued him relentlessly. At that time he traveled south from Pudong, intending to join Liangshan, but was waylaid while passing this mountain. Tang Bin then fought Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye, the leaders of the mountain stronghold. Neither man could defeat him, so they invited Tang Bin up the mountain and yielded the chieftainship to him. Last year, when Tian Hu seized Hugu Pass, he demanded Tang Bin’s submission. Tang Bin had no wish to yield, but, seeing how isolated and weak he was, reluctantly submitted. He has, however, remained stationed on his own mountain, serving as an outwork of Hugu Pass against the armies from the south. Recently, hearing that I had been stationed at Weizhou, Tang Bin secretly came alone on horseback to Weizhou on New Year’s Day and disclosed to me all that had long been in his heart. He has long admired Elder Brother’s loyalty and righteousness. He has always wished to submit to the imperial court, place himself under Elder Brother’s command, and redeem his offenses through meritorious service. I rode alone with Tang Bin to Mount Baodu and found Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye both frank and honorable men, without the slightest trace of anything base or mean. They too wish to submit. We secretly agreed that, when the opportunity arises, they will deliver up the pass as the means by which they may enter imperial service.”

p.src: Now Shan Shiqi secretly sent a man to arrange with Tang Bin to dispatch troops under cover. The messenger returned and reported, “The moon is now as bright as day. We should wait until the dark of the moon before advancing, so that the enemy will not notice us.” Shiqi said, “That is sound advice.” More than ten days passed without the Song army coming to attack. Presently Tang Bin reached the pass and paid his respects to Shan Shiqi. Tang Bin said, “At the third watch tonight, Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye will lead ten thousand men secretly out from east of Mount Baodu. The soldiers will wear soft armor and the horses will have their bells removed. They are certain to reach the rear of the Song encampment by dawn. Make haste to prepare here, then sally from the pass to support them.” Shiqi said delightedly, “Attacked from both sides, the Song troops are certain to be defeated!” Shiqi laid out wine and entertained him. At dusk, Tang Bin went up onto the pass to look about and said, “Strange. By the starlight, it seems someone is scouting outside the pass.” Even as he spoke, he took two arrows from the quiver of an attendant soldier and shot them beyond the pass. It was indeed fated that the pass should fall: several soldiers really were outside it, obeying the Song vanguard commander’s order to hide in the darkness and spy out news from within. One of Tang Bin’s arrows happened to strike a soldier in the right thigh, but though the flesh hurt, the arrow seemed to have no head. The soldier found this strange. Examining the arrow closely, he discovered that a quantity of silk was wrapped tightly around its head. Realizing there was some hidden message, the soldier raced back to camp and reported to the Song vanguard commander. Under the lamplight, Song Jiang unwrapped it and found several lines of tiny writing inside. It was a secret message from Tang Bin: “At dawn tomorrow I shall deliver up the pass. Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye will lead troops secretly to the rear of the vanguard’s camp. They will wait for the cannon signal, whereupon the men inside the pass will sally out to support them. At that moment Tang Bin will be among them and seize the opportunity to take the pass. I beg the Song vanguard commander to make haste and prepare to enter.” After reading it, Song Jiang secretly discussed the necessary preparations with Wu Yong. Wu Yong said, “General Guan’s judgment was evidently correct. Yet since the enemy troops will emerge behind us, we cannot leave ourselves unprepared. Order Sun Li, Zhu Tong, Shan Tinggui, Wei Dingguo, and Yan Shun to lead ten thousand men, furling their banners and silencing their drums, and move secretly behind the camp. If the forces of Generals Wen and Cui arrive, they must not be allowed to press suddenly upon the camp. Wait until our men have taken the pass and the thunderous linked signal cannon is fired; only then permit them to draw near. Next order Xu Ning and Suo Chao to lead five thousand men and secretly lie in ambush east of the camp; and Lin Chong and Zhang Qing to lead five thousand men and secretly lie in ambush west of the camp. At the sound of cannon fire within the camp, both forces are to emerge together in support, join their troops, and charge up to the pass. Should our men fall into the enemy’s treacherous scheme, they are to come at once to the rescue.” Song Jiang said, “An excellent plan, Strategist!” Orders were immediately issued according to this plan, and the generals went to make ready as commanded.

p.src: Meanwhile, inside the pass Shan Shiqi had received Tang Bin’s news and waited intently for cannon fire behind the Song encampment. At daybreak, a sudden succession of cannon shots sounded south of the pass. Tang Bin and Shiqi climbed up to survey the scene and saw dust rising behind the Song encampment and its banners in confusion. Tang Bin said, “The troops of Generals Wen and Cui must have arrived. Make haste to sally from the pass and support them!” Shan Shiqi and Shi Ding led ten thousand picked troops out first to attack. Tang Bin and Lu Hui were ordered to follow with another ten thousand in support, while Zhu Jing and Zhong Liang remained stationed on the pass. When the Song troops saw soldiers charging out from the pass, they hurriedly retreated toward their rear. Shan Shiqi drove his men forward at the head of the charge. Suddenly a cannon boomed, and two formidable bodies of cavalry burst out on either side of the Song troops and came charging to attack. Seeing the two Song forces attack, Tang Bin swiftly wheeled his horse around, led his troops back toward the pass, and halted outside the gate with spear leveled from horseback. While Shan Shiqi and Shi Ding were fighting in separate quarters, another cannon sounded in the Song camp. Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun came surging forward with their javelin-and-shield men. Shan Shiqi realized that preparations had been made against him and hastily recalled his troops, wheeling his horse toward the pass. A general before the pass sat his horse and cried aloud, “Tang Bin is here! Hugu Pass now belongs to the Song court. Shan Shiqi, dismount and surrender at once!” With a single thrust of his spear, he had already stabbed Zhu Jing to death. Shan Shiqi was aghast and knew not what to do. Leading several dozen horsemen, he fought desperately westward and broke through. Lin Chong and Zhang Qing wished to seize the pass, so they did not pursue him but led their troops in an assault upon it. By then Li Kui and the other light-footed infantrymen had already scrambled onto the pass. They fired the signal cannon and, together with Tang Bin, cut down the defending soldiers and seized Hugu Pass. Zhong Liang was killed amid the melee. Outside the pass, Shi Ding was knocked from his horse by Xu Ning. The northern troops scattered and fled, abandoning countless suits of armor and horses. More than two thousand were killed, over five hundred captured alive, and a great many surrendered.

p.src: Presently the main body under the Song vanguard commanders entered the pass in succession. Tang Bin dismounted, bowed before Song Jiang, and said, “I, Tang, am a convicted man. Hearing of your benevolence and righteousness, Commander, I wished even then to seek refuge in your great camp, but had no means of access and could not behold your honored countenance. Today, thanks to this opportunity granted by Heaven, I have been able to follow at your bridle and stirrup, fulfilling the wish of my life.” When he had finished, he bowed again. Song Jiang repeatedly returned his courtesies, hastily helped him up, and said, “General, now that you have submitted to the court, join me in sweeping away the rebels. When I return to court, I shall commend you to the Son of Heaven, and you will naturally receive generous advancement.” Afterward Sun Li and the other generals, together with Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye, led the two bodies of troops and encamped outside the pass to await orders. Song Jiang sent orders for Generals Wen and Cui to enter the pass and meet him. Sun Li and the others remained in command of the troops and encamped outside the pass for the time being. Wen Zhongrong and Cui Ye entered the pass, bowed before the Song vanguard commander, and said, “We, Wen and Cui, are fortunate to have the chance to serve beneath your banner and wish to render the service of dogs and horses.” Song Jiang said with great delight, “You generals helped take this pass by stratagem; your merit is considerable. I shall record every deed in the register of merit.” The next day he ordered a banquet prepared to celebrate with Tang Bin and the other two men. Meanwhile the soldiers inside and outside the pass were counted. There were more than twenty thousand newly surrendered troops and over a thousand captured warhorses. All the generals came forward to report their achievements.

p.src: The tale now divides into two threads. Meanwhile, the officials of the rebel provincial administration at Weisheng received urgent dispatches from Shan Shiqi, commander at Huguan Pass, and Tian Biao at Jinning. They reported the matter to Tian Hu, saying that the Song army was overwhelmingly strong and both Huguan and Jinning were in grave danger. Tian Hu ascended the hall and conferred with his followers about sending troops to their aid. Just then a man stepped out from the assembled ranks. He wore a yellow Daoist cap and a crane-feather cloak. Coming forward, he memorialized, “My lord, I beg leave to go to Huguan and drive back the enemy.” The man’s surname was Qiao, and his given name was Lie. His family had originally come from Jingyuan in Shaanxi. While his mother was pregnant, she dreamed that a jackal entered her chamber and afterward changed into a deer. Upon waking from the dream, she gave birth to Lie. At eight years old, Qiao Lie already delighted in wielding spear and staff. Once, while roaming Mount Kongtong, he met a mysterious adept who taught him magical arts, enabling him to summon wind and rain and ride upon mist and cloud. He once went to Mount Erxian in Jiugong County to seek the Way, but Perfected Luo refused to receive him. Instead, he sent a young Daoist with this message: “You labor at heterodox arts without comprehending the profound mystery. When virtue has subdued your demonic nature, then you may come and see me.” Qiao Lie returned in anger. Trusting in his magical powers, he wandered about without restraint. Because he possessed so many magical arts, everyone called him the “Demon Lord of Illusions.” Later he came to Anding Prefecture. The prefecture was suffering from a severe drought: for five months not a drop of rain had fallen. The prefectural authorities posted a proclamation: “Whoever can pray down life-giving rain shall receive a guaranteed reward of three thousand strings of cash.” Qiao Lie tore down the proclamation, mounted the altar, and brought down a great, sweet rain. Once the prefectural officer saw that ample rain had fallen, he ceased to give the promised reward any thought. But Qiao Lie was fated to meet with trouble. There was a crooked scholar in the prefecture named He Cai, who was very close to the treasury clerk. When he learned what had happened, he urged the clerk to present most of the reward money to the prefectural officer and embezzle the rest for themselves. He Cai had financial dealings with the treasury clerk and managed to skim off a little profit himself. The treasury clerk handed Qiao Lie only three strings of cash and said, “With such lofty arts as yours, you have no use for this money anyway. Here, even the regular taxes and provisions that must be dispatched are still insufficient, and we have to scrape them together from every quarter. If you take my advice, leave this reward money in the treasury for the time being. Whenever you need it later, you may come and draw it out little by little.” When Qiao Lie heard this, he flew into a rage. “The money for this promised reward was contributed by the wealthy households of the prefecture. How dare you embezzle it at will? The grain and funds in the treasury are all wrung from the people’s flesh and blood, yet you care for nothing but stealing them to fatten yourself, buying laughter and chasing pleasure, thereby ruining countless affairs of state. If I beat a filthy wretch like you to death, I shall also rid the treasury of a pest!” He raised his fists and struck the clerk squarely in the face. The treasury clerk had been hollowed out by wine and women and was also grossly fat. He was panting before the fight had even begun, so how could he ward off the blows? Qiao Lie pummeled and kicked him savagely. The clerk staggered home in a wretched state, lay bedridden for four or five days, and then, alas, died of his severe injuries. The treasury clerk’s wife and children lodged a formal complaint with the prefectural authorities. The prefectural officer was already fairly certain that the affair had arisen over the promised reward. He endorsed an official warrant and sent men to arrest the killer, Qiao Lie, and bring him in for questioning.

p.src: The four subordinate generals were each nominally appointed to the office of commander. Following Qiao Daoqing and leading two thousand picked troops, they marched day and night toward Zhaode. In less than a day they came within ten li north of Zhaode, where a mounted scout from the vanguard reported, “Yesterday the Song forces broke through Huguan. They have now divided into three columns and are attacking the city of Zhaode.” On hearing the report, Qiao Daoqing flew into a rage. “How dare those scoundrels behave so insolently! I shall teach them what I can do!” He led his troops forward at full speed. They came upon Tang Bin and Geng Gong leading their troops in an assault on the north gate. Suddenly word came that more than two thousand horsemen were approaching from the northwest, and Tang Bin and Geng Gong drew up their formation to meet the enemy. Qiao Daoqing’s forces soon arrived. The two armies faced each other, banners and drums visible across the field, with scarcely a bowshot separating north from south. Tang Bin and Geng Gong saw four officers before the northern formation clustered around a Taoist master, who sat his horse beneath a crimson silk canopy. What manner of man was this master? Upon his head he wore a fishtail Taoist cap of purple gold inset with jewels. He was clad in a brocade crane-feather cloak patterned with flames and edged in black, with a many-colored silken cord tied about his waist and square crimson shoes with cloud-shaped toes upon his feet. He wielded an ancient Kunwu-iron sword and rode a silver-maned, snow-dappled horse. His brows spread like the character eight, his eyes were blue, and a thick beard hung from his face; his mouth was broad and square, and his voice rang like a bell.

p.src: On the black banner before the master’s horse, nineteen great characters were written in gold in two lines: “Divinely Responsive Perfected One, Protector of the Realm; Military Counselor and Left Chancellor; Grand Marshal for the Southern Campaign, Qiao.” After reading it, Geng Gong said in alarm, “This man is formidable!” Before the two armies could engage, Li Kui and his five hundred skirmishers suddenly arrived. Li Kui made to charge forward, but Geng Gong said, “This man is the ablest of all the Prince of Jin’s followers. He commands sorcery and is exceedingly dangerous.” Li Kui said, “I’ll rush up and hack that bird-brained wretch down. Then let’s see what damned trick he can use!” Tang Bin also warned him, “General, you must not underestimate the enemy.” But Li Kui would not listen. Brandishing his broad axes, he charged into the attack. Fearing some mishap might befall him, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun led the five hundred shield-and-javelin men surging forward together. The master laughed aloud and shouted, “Do not run wild, you scoundrel!” Without the least haste, he pointed his precious sword toward the sky, muttered an incantation, and cried, “Now!” Though it had been broad daylight beneath a clear blue sky, in an instant dense black fog spread everywhere, a fierce wind howled, and dust and earth flew through the air. Another mass of black vapor enveloped Li Kui and his five hundred men. It was as though they had been swept into a pitch-black leather sack: not the slightest glimmer could be seen before their eyes, nor could they move so much as an inch. They heard only the sound of wind and rain beside their ears and had no idea where they were. Hero or mighty champion though you be, you cannot sprout wings and soar away. Even if you were the Fire-Headed Vajra, how could you escape this net spread over earth and sky? Even Eight-Armed Nezha could hardly break free from this dragon’s pool and tiger’s den. To learn what peril befell Li Kui and the others, and whether they lived or died, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
